title: MCAT: Biochemistry Essentials

sources.name: Original educational writing from general knowledge
OpenStax Biology 2e: macromolecules and enzymes (limited factual spot checks; original card wording)

description: For MCAT learners reviewing amino acids, proteins, enzymes, metabolism, nucleic acids, and lab methods. Educational biochemical principles; verify with current guidelines for clinical applications.

cards.front: What are the three-letter and one-letter codes for glycine?
cards.back: Gly and G.

cards.front: Which amino acid has the one-letter code G?
cards.back: Glycine (Gly).

cards.front: What distinguishes the side chain of glycine?
cards.back: A hydrogen side chain; the only standard amino acid with an achiral alpha carbon.

cards.front: What are the three-letter and one-letter codes for alanine?
cards.back: Ala and A.

cards.front: Which amino acid has the one-letter code A?
cards.back: Alanine (Ala).

cards.front: What distinguishes the side chain of alanine?
cards.back: A methyl side chain; nonpolar and small.

cards.front: What are the three-letter and one-letter codes for valine?
cards.back: Val and V.

cards.front: Which amino acid has the one-letter code V?
cards.back: Valine (Val).

cards.front: What distinguishes the side chain of valine?
cards.back: A branched isopropyl side chain; nonpolar and essential in the diet.

cards.front: What are the three-letter and one-letter codes for leucine?
cards.back: Leu and L.

cards.front: Which amino acid has the one-letter code L?
cards.back: Leucine (Leu).

cards.front: What distinguishes the side chain of leucine?
cards.back: A branched isobutyl side chain; nonpolar and exclusively ketogenic.

cards.front: What are the three-letter and one-letter codes for isoleucine?
cards.back: Ile and I.

cards.front: Which amino acid has the one-letter code I?
cards.back: Isoleucine (Ile).

cards.front: What distinguishes the side chain of isoleucine?
cards.back: A branched sec-butyl side chain; nonpolar and has a second stereocenter.

cards.front: What are the three-letter and one-letter codes for methionine?
cards.back: Met and M.

cards.front: Which amino acid has the one-letter code M?
cards.back: Methionine (Met).

cards.front: What distinguishes the side chain of methionine?
cards.back: A sulfur-containing thioether side chain; nonpolar and often the first residue translated.

cards.front: What are the three-letter and one-letter codes for proline?
cards.back: Pro and P.

cards.front: Which amino acid has the one-letter code P?
cards.back: Proline (Pro).

cards.front: What distinguishes the side chain of proline?
cards.back: A side chain that joins the backbone nitrogen, restricting backbone rotation.

cards.front: What are the three-letter and one-letter codes for phenylalanine?
cards.back: Phe and F.

cards.front: Which amino acid has the one-letter code F?
cards.back: Phenylalanine (Phe).

cards.front: What distinguishes the side chain of phenylalanine?
cards.back: A benzyl side chain; aromatic and largely hydrophobic.

cards.front: What are the three-letter and one-letter codes for tyrosine?
cards.back: Tyr and Y.

cards.front: Which amino acid has the one-letter code Y?
cards.back: Tyrosine (Tyr).

cards.front: What distinguishes the side chain of tyrosine?
cards.back: An aromatic phenol side chain that can be phosphorylated.

cards.front: What are the three-letter and one-letter codes for tryptophan?
cards.back: Trp and W.

cards.front: Which amino acid has the one-letter code W?
cards.back: Tryptophan (Trp).

cards.front: What distinguishes the side chain of tryptophan?
cards.back: An indole side chain; aromatic and a strong contributor to protein absorbance at 280 nm.

cards.front: What are the three-letter and one-letter codes for serine?
cards.back: Ser and S.

cards.front: Which amino acid has the one-letter code S?
cards.back: Serine (Ser).

cards.front: What distinguishes the side chain of serine?
cards.back: A hydroxymethyl side chain; polar and a common phosphorylation site.

cards.front: What are the three-letter and one-letter codes for threonine?
cards.back: Thr and T.

cards.front: Which amino acid has the one-letter code T?
cards.back: Threonine (Thr).

cards.front: What distinguishes the side chain of threonine?
cards.back: A hydroxyl-bearing side chain with a second stereocenter; a common phosphorylation site.

cards.front: What are the three-letter and one-letter codes for cysteine?
cards.back: Cys and C.

cards.front: Which amino acid has the one-letter code C?
cards.back: Cysteine (Cys).

cards.front: What distinguishes the side chain of cysteine?
cards.back: A thiol side chain that can form disulfide bonds upon oxidation.

cards.front: What are the three-letter and one-letter codes for asparagine?
cards.back: Asn and N.

cards.front: Which amino acid has the one-letter code N?
cards.back: Asparagine (Asn).

cards.front: What distinguishes the side chain of asparagine?
cards.back: A carboxamide side chain; polar and ordinarily uncharged near physiological pH.

cards.front: What are the three-letter and one-letter codes for glutamine?
cards.back: Gln and Q.

cards.front: Which amino acid has the one-letter code Q?
cards.back: Glutamine (Gln).

cards.front: What distinguishes the side chain of glutamine?
cards.back: An amide side chain one methylene longer than asparagine's; an important nitrogen carrier.

cards.front: What are the three-letter and one-letter codes for aspartate?
cards.back: Asp and D.

cards.front: Which amino acid has the one-letter code D?
cards.back: Aspartate (Asp).

cards.front: What distinguishes the side chain of aspartate?
cards.back: A side-chain carboxylate, ordinarily negatively charged near physiological pH.

cards.front: What are the three-letter and one-letter codes for glutamate?
cards.back: Glu and E.

cards.front: Which amino acid has the one-letter code E?
cards.back: Glutamate (Glu).

cards.front: What distinguishes the side chain of glutamate?
cards.back: A side-chain carboxylate one methylene longer than aspartate's; ordinarily negatively charged near physiological pH.

cards.front: What are the three-letter and one-letter codes for lysine?
cards.back: Lys and K.

cards.front: Which amino acid has the one-letter code K?
cards.back: Lysine (Lys).

cards.front: What distinguishes the side chain of lysine?
cards.back: A terminal amino group on a four-methylene chain; ordinarily positively charged near physiological pH.

cards.front: What are the three-letter and one-letter codes for arginine?
cards.back: Arg and R.

cards.front: Which amino acid has the one-letter code R?
cards.back: Arginine (Arg).

cards.front: What distinguishes the side chain of arginine?
cards.back: A guanidinium side chain; ordinarily positively charged near physiological pH.

cards.front: What are the three-letter and one-letter codes for histidine?
cards.back: His and H.

cards.front: Which amino acid has the one-letter code H?
cards.back: Histidine (His).

cards.front: What distinguishes the side chain of histidine?
cards.back: An imidazole side chain with a pKa near 6 in free solution; useful in acid-base catalysis.

cards.front: What groups attach to the alpha carbon of a typical free alpha-amino acid?
cards.back: An amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen, and a side chain; glycine has hydrogen as its side chain.

cards.front: What is a zwitterion?
cards.back: A molecule carrying both positive and negative formal charges while having zero net charge.

cards.front: What does an amino acid's isoelectric point mean?
cards.back: The pH at which its average net charge is zero.

cards.front: Below its isoelectric point, what net charge does an amino acid tend to have?
cards.back: A positive net charge because more groups are protonated.

cards.front: Above its isoelectric point, what net charge does an amino acid tend to have?
cards.back: A negative net charge because more groups are deprotonated.

cards.front: What equation relates pH, pKa, and conjugate acid/base concentrations?
cards.back: pH = pKa + log10([conjugate base]/[acid]).

cards.front: At pH equal to pKa, how do conjugate base and acid concentrations compare?
cards.back: Their concentrations are equal.

cards.front: How is the pI calculated for a simple amino acid without an ionizable side chain?
cards.back: Average the pKa values of the alpha-carboxyl and alpha-ammonium groups.

cards.front: How do you select pKa values to calculate pI when a side chain is ionizable?
cards.back: Average the two pKa values that bracket the net-neutral species.

cards.front: Which configuration predominates among amino acids incorporated into human proteins?
cards.back: L configuration; glycine is achiral.

cards.front: Does L configuration always mean S absolute configuration for protein amino acids?
cards.back: No. Cysteine is normally R because sulfur changes priority ordering; glycine has no R/S configuration.

cards.front: What bond joins amino acid residues in a protein?
cards.back: A peptide bond, an amide linkage between a carboxyl carbon and an amino nitrogen.

cards.front: Why is a peptide bond approximately planar?
cards.back: Resonance gives the carbon-nitrogen bond partial double-bond character and restricts rotation.

cards.front: How is a peptide sequence conventionally written?
cards.back: From the amino terminus, or N terminus, to the carboxyl terminus, or C terminus.

cards.front: What defines protein primary structure?
cards.back: The amino acid sequence, with covalent connectivity such as disulfide links also relevant to full structural description.

cards.front: What stabilizes an alpha helix's backbone?
cards.back: Hydrogen bonds between a backbone carbonyl oxygen and the backbone N-H four residues later.

cards.front: What stabilizes beta-sheet secondary structure?
cards.back: Hydrogen bonds between backbone groups of neighboring beta strands.

cards.front: How do parallel and antiparallel beta sheets differ?
cards.back: Neighboring strands run in the same N-to-C direction in parallel sheets and opposite directions in antiparallel sheets.

cards.front: What defines protein tertiary structure?
cards.back: The overall three-dimensional fold of a single polypeptide chain.

cards.front: What defines protein quaternary structure?
cards.back: The arrangement of multiple polypeptide subunits in a functional complex.

cards.front: What drives hydrophobic side chains toward a soluble protein's interior?
cards.back: The hydrophobic effect: burying nonpolar surfaces generally releases ordered surrounding water.

cards.front: What is a disulfide bond in a protein?
cards.back: A covalent sulfur-sulfur bond produced by oxidation of two cysteine thiols.

cards.front: Does ordinary protein denaturation cleave the peptide backbone?
cards.back: Usually no. It disrupts higher-order structure while generally retaining the primary sequence.

cards.front: What do molecular chaperones do?
cards.back: Help proteins fold or avoid aggregation without specifying the amino acid sequence.

cards.front: Why does proline often disrupt an internal alpha helix?
cards.back: Its constrained backbone and lack of a backbone N-H donor interfere with regular helix geometry and hydrogen bonding.

cards.front: Why can glycine favor flexible turns in proteins?
cards.back: Its tiny side chain permits a wide range of backbone conformations.

cards.front: What is the main structural protein of connective tissue?
cards.back: Collagen, commonly arranged as three polypeptide chains in a triple helix.

cards.front: Why is glycine frequent in collagen's repeating sequence?
cards.back: Its small size permits tight packing at the center of the triple helix.

cards.front: Which vitamin supports hydroxylation of proline and lysine during collagen maturation?
cards.back: Vitamin C, which helps maintain iron in the required reduced state for the hydroxylases.

cards.front: How does myoglobin's oxygen-binding curve differ from hemoglobin's?
cards.back: Myoglobin has a hyperbolic curve; cooperative hemoglobin has a sigmoidal curve.

cards.front: What does positive cooperativity mean in hemoglobin?
cards.back: Binding one oxygen molecule increases the affinity of other subunits for oxygen.

cards.front: What does a right shift of the hemoglobin oxygen-binding curve indicate?
cards.back: Lower oxygen affinity and greater oxygen unloading at a given oxygen partial pressure.

cards.front: What is the Bohr effect?
cards.back: Higher carbon dioxide or lower pH reduces hemoglobin's oxygen affinity, favoring oxygen release.

cards.front: How does 2,3-BPG affect adult hemoglobin?
cards.back: It stabilizes the deoxygenated state and lowers oxygen affinity.

cards.front: Why does fetal hemoglobin generally bind oxygen more tightly than adult hemoglobin?
cards.back: Its gamma-containing structure binds 2,3-BPG less strongly, favoring higher oxygen affinity.

cards.front: What distinguishes an enzyme's active site from an allosteric site?
cards.back: The active site binds substrates and supports catalysis; an allosteric site binds regulators that alter activity.

cards.front: What does a catalyst change about a reaction's energy profile?
cards.back: It lowers activation free energy, increasing reaction rate.

cards.front: Does an enzyme change the reaction's equilibrium constant?
cards.back: No. It speeds approach to equilibrium without changing the equilibrium constant or overall free-energy change.

cards.front: What is induced fit in enzyme binding?
cards.back: Substrate binding promotes a conformational adjustment that helps form a catalytically effective complex.

cards.front: What is the Michaelis-Menten equation?
cards.back: v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) for a simple Michaelis-Menten system under its initial-rate assumptions.

cards.front: What is Km operationally in Michaelis-Menten kinetics?
cards.back: The substrate concentration at which initial velocity is half of Vmax.

cards.front: Is Km always identical to the substrate dissociation constant?
cards.back: No. Km includes binding and catalytic rate constants; it approximates the dissociation constant only under suitable kinetic conditions.

cards.front: What is Vmax?
cards.back: The limiting initial reaction rate when the enzyme is saturated with substrate.

cards.front: How does doubling enzyme concentration affect Vmax, all else equal?
cards.back: Vmax doubles; Km is unchanged in the simple Michaelis-Menten model.

cards.front: What is kcat?
cards.back: The turnover number, Vmax divided by the concentration of active enzyme sites.

cards.front: What does kcat/Km measure?
cards.back: Catalytic efficiency in the low-substrate regime.

cards.front: How does competitive inhibition affect apparent Km and Vmax?
cards.back: It raises apparent Km while leaving Vmax unchanged in the classical reversible model.

cards.front: Can sufficient substrate overcome classical reversible competitive inhibition?
cards.back: Yes, the uninhibited Vmax can still be approached at sufficiently high substrate concentration.

cards.front: How does pure noncompetitive inhibition affect Km and Vmax?
cards.back: It lowers Vmax without changing Km because inhibitor affinity for free enzyme and enzyme-substrate complex is equal.

cards.front: How does uncompetitive inhibition affect apparent Km and Vmax?
cards.back: It lowers both by the same factor in the classical model.

cards.front: What species does an uncompetitive inhibitor bind?
cards.back: The enzyme-substrate complex rather than free enzyme.

cards.front: What is mixed inhibition?
cards.back: An inhibitor binds both free enzyme and enzyme-substrate complex with unequal affinities, lowering Vmax and changing apparent Km.

cards.front: What is irreversible enzyme inhibition?
cards.back: Persistent loss of enzyme activity, often through covalent modification or extremely tight binding.

cards.front: What are the axes of a Lineweaver-Burk plot?
cards.back: 1/v on the vertical axis and 1/[S] on the horizontal axis.

cards.front: What are the Lineweaver-Burk intercepts for Michaelis-Menten kinetics?
cards.back: The y-intercept is 1/Vmax; the x-intercept is -1/Km.

cards.front: What is feedback inhibition?
cards.back: A downstream product inhibits an earlier pathway step, often the first committed step.

cards.front: What is a zymogen?
cards.back: An inactive enzyme precursor activated by a modification such as proteolytic cleavage.

cards.front: What distinguishes a coenzyme from an inorganic cofactor?
cards.back: A coenzyme is an organic helper molecule; inorganic cofactors include metal ions.

cards.front: What is a prosthetic group?
cards.back: A nonprotein component tightly associated with a protein and needed for its function.

cards.front: What reaction class do oxidoreductases catalyze?
cards.back: Electron-transfer reactions, including oxidation and reduction.

cards.front: What reaction class do transferases catalyze?
cards.back: Transfer of functional groups between molecules.

cards.front: What reaction class do hydrolases catalyze?
cards.back: Bond cleavage using water.

cards.front: What reaction class do lyases catalyze?
cards.back: Nonhydrolytic, nonoxidative bond cleavage or addition across a double bond.

cards.front: What reaction class do isomerases catalyze?
cards.back: Rearrangements within a molecule to produce an isomer.

cards.front: What reaction class do ligases catalyze?
cards.back: Joining molecules, commonly coupled to ATP or another nucleotide triphosphate's hydrolysis.

cards.front: What do kinases generally transfer?
cards.back: A phosphoryl group, often from ATP to a substrate.

cards.front: What do phosphatases generally remove?
cards.back: Phosphate groups by hydrolysis.

cards.front: What is oxidation in biochemical electron transfer?
cards.back: Loss of electrons; often loss of hydrogen or gain of bonds to oxygen.

cards.front: What is reduction in biochemical electron transfer?
cards.back: Gain of electrons; often gain of hydrogen or loss of bonds to oxygen.

cards.front: What is the Gibbs free-energy relation involving enthalpy and entropy?
cards.back: Delta G = delta H - T delta S, with temperature in kelvin.

cards.front: What does a negative delta G indicate?
cards.back: The forward reaction is thermodynamically favorable under the specified conditions; it need not be fast.

cards.front: How does actual delta G relate to standard transformed delta G and reaction quotient?
cards.back: Delta G = delta G standard transformed + RT ln Q, using a consistent biochemical convention.

cards.front: What is delta G at equilibrium?
cards.back: Zero; there is no net thermodynamic driving force.

cards.front: How can ATP hydrolysis drive an unfavorable reaction?
cards.back: Coupling reactions through a shared mechanism can make the combined free-energy change negative.

cards.front: What is substrate-level phosphorylation?
cards.back: ATP or GTP formation by direct phosphate transfer from an energy-rich substrate.

cards.front: What is oxidative phosphorylation?
cards.back: ATP production coupled to electron transport through an electrochemical proton gradient.

cards.front: Where does glycolysis occur in human cells?
cards.back: In the cytosol.

cards.front: What is the net ATP yield of glycolysis per glucose?
cards.back: Two ATP: four produced minus two consumed.

cards.front: What are the principal net products of glycolysis per glucose?
cards.back: Two pyruvate, two ATP, and two NADH, with water and protons depending on equation convention.

cards.front: Which glycolytic enzyme traps glucose as glucose-6-phosphate in most tissues?
cards.back: Hexokinase; glucokinase performs a related role in liver and pancreatic beta cells.

cards.front: How does glucokinase differ functionally from many hexokinase isoforms?
cards.back: It has a higher glucose concentration requirement and is not inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate.

cards.front: Which enzyme catalyzes glycolysis's committed regulatory step?
cards.back: Phosphofructokinase-1, converting fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.

cards.front: How does ATP regulate phosphofructokinase-1 at high energy charge?
cards.back: High ATP inhibits its activity allosterically.

cards.front: How does fructose-2,6-bisphosphate affect phosphofructokinase-1?
cards.back: It activates phosphofructokinase-1, promoting glycolysis.

cards.front: Which glycolytic reaction produces NADH?
cards.back: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase converts glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate.

cards.front: Which two glycolytic enzymes directly generate ATP?
cards.back: Phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase.

cards.front: Why is lactate production useful when oxidative NADH reoxidation is limited?
cards.back: Lactate dehydrogenase regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue.

cards.front: Does conversion of pyruvate to lactate directly produce extra ATP?
cards.back: No. It regenerates NAD+; ATP comes from glycolysis.

cards.front: Where is the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex located in human cells?
cards.back: The mitochondrial matrix.

cards.front: What does pyruvate dehydrogenase produce from pyruvate?
cards.back: Acetyl-CoA, carbon dioxide, and NADH.

cards.front: Which five cofactors are classically associated with pyruvate dehydrogenase?
cards.back: Thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoamide, coenzyme A, FAD, and NAD+.

cards.front: Is pyruvate dehydrogenase normally reversible in human metabolism?
cards.back: No. It is effectively irreversible under physiological conditions.

cards.front: Where do most citric acid cycle reactions occur in human cells?
cards.back: The mitochondrial matrix; succinate dehydrogenase is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

cards.front: What molecules combine in the citrate synthase reaction?
cards.back: Acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate form citrate, releasing coenzyme A.

cards.front: What is the net reduced-cofactor yield per acetyl-CoA in the citric acid cycle?
cards.back: Three NADH and one FADH2 equivalent, with one GTP or ATP and two carbon dioxide also produced.

cards.front: Which citric acid cycle enzyme also serves as electron transport complex II?
cards.back: Succinate dehydrogenase.

cards.front: Which citric acid cycle reaction generates GTP or ATP directly?
cards.back: Conversion of succinyl-CoA to succinate by succinyl-CoA synthetase.

cards.front: What does an anaplerotic reaction do?
cards.back: Replenishes intermediates removed from a metabolic cycle, especially the citric acid cycle.

cards.front: What does pyruvate carboxylase make?
cards.back: Oxaloacetate from pyruvate, using ATP and bicarbonate with biotin as a cofactor.

cards.front: What allosterically activates pyruvate carboxylase?
cards.back: Acetyl-CoA.

cards.front: Where is the respiratory electron transport chain in mitochondria?
cards.back: In the inner mitochondrial membrane.

cards.front: Which respiratory complexes pump protons in the standard mitochondrial chain?
cards.back: Complexes I, III, and IV; complex II does not.

cards.front: What is the terminal electron acceptor of the mitochondrial respiratory chain?
cards.back: Oxygen, which is reduced to water at complex IV.

cards.front: What carries electrons from complexes I or II to complex III?
cards.back: Coenzyme Q, also called ubiquinone in its oxidized form.

cards.front: What carries electrons from complex III to complex IV?
cards.back: Cytochrome c.

cards.front: What directly powers ATP synthase during oxidative phosphorylation?
cards.back: Proton flow down the electrochemical gradient through the enzyme.

cards.front: How does an uncoupler affect mitochondrial ATP production?
cards.back: It dissipates the proton gradient, reducing ATP synthesis while electron transport can continue or accelerate.

cards.front: Why is inner mitochondrial membrane integrity important for ATP production?
cards.back: The membrane must retain a proton gradient for chemiosmotic coupling.

cards.front: What is the usual approximate ATP yield per mitochondrial NADH oxidized?
cards.back: About 2.5 ATP, with actual yield depending on coupling and cellular conditions.

cards.front: What is the usual approximate ATP yield per FADH2 equivalent entering at complex II?
cards.back: About 1.5 ATP, because complex I proton pumping is bypassed.

cards.front: Why do cytosolic NADH shuttle pathways affect the calculated ATP yield from glucose?
cards.back: The shuttles transfer reducing equivalents into mitochondria at different entry points in electron transport.

cards.front: What is gluconeogenesis?
cards.back: Synthesis of glucose from noncarbohydrate precursors such as lactate, glycerol, and glucogenic amino acids.

cards.front: Which organs contribute most to human gluconeogenesis?
cards.back: The liver is primary; the kidneys contribute, especially during prolonged fasting.

cards.front: Can acetyl-CoA from even-chain fatty acids yield net glucose in humans?
cards.back: No. Humans lack a pathway for net conversion of those acetyl units into glucose.

cards.front: Which enzymes bypass pyruvate kinase during gluconeogenesis?
cards.back: Pyruvate carboxylase and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase.

cards.front: Which gluconeogenic enzyme bypasses phosphofructokinase-1?
cards.back: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase.

cards.front: Which gluconeogenic enzyme releases free glucose from glucose-6-phosphate?
cards.back: Glucose-6-phosphatase.

cards.front: Why cannot skeletal muscle normally release substantial free glucose from glycogen?
cards.back: It lacks glucose-6-phosphatase and uses its glycogen mainly for local energy needs.

cards.front: What is the Cori cycle?
cards.back: Lactate produced by tissues such as muscle or red blood cells travels to the liver for conversion back to glucose.

cards.front: What are glycogen's main glycosidic linkages?
cards.back: Alpha-1,4 bonds in chains and alpha-1,6 bonds at branch points.

cards.front: Which enzyme elongates glycogen chains?
cards.back: Glycogen synthase, using UDP-glucose as the activated donor.

cards.front: Which enzyme cleaves glycogen's alpha-1,4 bonds by phosphorolysis?
cards.back: Glycogen phosphorylase, releasing glucose-1-phosphate.

cards.front: What additional activity is needed to remove glycogen branch points?
cards.back: Debranching enzyme activities, including transferase and alpha-1,6-glucosidase functions.

cards.front: How does insulin generally affect glycogen metabolism?
cards.back: It favors glycogen synthesis and reduces glycogen breakdown.

cards.front: How does glucagon generally affect hepatic glucose output?
cards.back: It promotes glucose production and release by stimulating glycogenolysis and gluconeogenic regulation.

cards.front: Where does the pentose phosphate pathway occur?
cards.back: In the cytosol.

cards.front: What are the key products of the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway?
cards.back: NADPH and ribulose-5-phosphate, with carbon dioxide released.

cards.front: What is a major biosynthetic use of ribose-5-phosphate?
cards.back: Synthesis of nucleotides.

cards.front: How does NADPH help defend cells against oxidant stress?
cards.back: It supports regeneration of reduced glutathione through glutathione reductase.

cards.front: Which enzyme catalyzes the first oxidative pentose phosphate pathway step?
cards.back: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase.

cards.front: Which vitamin-derived cofactor does transketolase require?
cards.back: Thiamine pyrophosphate, derived from vitamin B1.

cards.front: What is a triacylglycerol?
cards.back: Glycerol esterified to three fatty acids; a major storage lipid.

cards.front: What makes a fatty acid saturated?
cards.back: It contains no carbon-carbon double bonds in its hydrocarbon chain.

cards.front: How do cis double bonds affect fatty acid packing?
cards.back: They introduce bends, reduce tight packing, and generally lower melting temperature.

cards.front: What makes a molecule amphipathic?
cards.back: It has both hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions.

cards.front: Why do phospholipids form bilayers in water?
cards.back: Their polar heads interact with water while hydrophobic tails cluster away from water.

cards.front: What does cholesterol do to animal membrane fluidity?
cards.back: It buffers fluidity: restrains lipid movement at higher temperatures and limits tight packing at lower temperatures.

cards.front: Where does mitochondrial beta-oxidation occur?
cards.back: Primarily in the mitochondrial matrix after fatty acid activation and appropriate transport.

cards.front: What does the carnitine shuttle transport into mitochondria?
cards.back: Long-chain fatty acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane.

cards.front: What inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase I?
cards.back: Malonyl-CoA, helping prevent simultaneous fatty acid synthesis and mitochondrial oxidation.

cards.front: What are the recurring reaction types in beta-oxidation?
cards.back: Oxidation, hydration, oxidation, and thiolysis.

cards.front: What does one standard beta-oxidation cycle produce?
cards.back: One NADH, one FADH2 equivalent, one acetyl-CoA, and an acyl-CoA shortened by two carbons; the final cycle yields two acetyl-CoA.

cards.front: What is the ATP-equivalent cost of fatty acid activation?
cards.back: Two ATP equivalents because ATP is converted to AMP and pyrophosphate.

cards.front: What is the final three-carbon product of odd-chain fatty acid oxidation?
cards.back: Propionyl-CoA, which can be converted to succinyl-CoA.

cards.front: Which vitamins support conversion of propionyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA?
cards.back: Biotin for carboxylation and vitamin B12 for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.

cards.front: Where does de novo fatty acid synthesis mainly occur?
cards.back: In the cytosol, especially in tissues such as liver and adipose tissue.

cards.front: Which enzyme makes malonyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis?
cards.back: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase, using ATP, bicarbonate, and biotin.

cards.front: Which reducing cofactor does fatty acid synthesis use?
cards.back: NADPH.

cards.front: What is the usual principal product of mammalian fatty acid synthase?
cards.back: Palmitate, a saturated 16-carbon fatty acid.

cards.front: What transports acetyl units from mitochondria for cytosolic fatty acid synthesis?
cards.back: Citrate export followed by cleavage by ATP-citrate lyase.

cards.front: Where are ketone bodies synthesized?
cards.back: In liver mitochondria from acetyl-CoA, especially when fatty acid oxidation is high.

cards.front: Name the three commonly listed ketone bodies.
cards.back: Acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate, and acetone; beta-hydroxybutyrate is not chemically a ketone.

cards.front: Why does the liver export rather than oxidize ketone bodies for energy?
cards.back: It lacks succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase, often called thiophorase or SCOT.

cards.front: Why cannot mature human red blood cells use ketone bodies or fatty acids for oxidative ATP production?
cards.back: They lack mitochondria and rely on glycolysis for ATP.

cards.front: What is transamination?
cards.back: Transfer of an amino group between an amino acid and a keto acid.

cards.front: Which vitamin-derived cofactor is required by aminotransferases?
cards.back: Pyridoxal phosphate, derived from vitamin B6.

cards.front: What nitrogen carrier commonly collects amino groups in transamination?
cards.back: Glutamate, formed by transfer of an amino group to alpha-ketoglutarate.

cards.front: What is the principal purpose of the urea cycle?
cards.back: Conversion of nitrogen waste to urea for excretion.

cards.front: Where does the urea cycle occur?
cards.back: Its steps span the mitochondrial matrix and cytosol, primarily in the liver.

cards.front: What are the two nitrogen sources in urea?
cards.back: Free ammonia, entering as carbamoyl phosphate, and aspartate.

cards.front: Which enzyme initiates the mitochondrial urea cycle?
cards.back: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I.

cards.front: What activates carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I?
cards.back: N-acetylglutamate.

cards.front: Which two amino acids are exclusively ketogenic?
cards.back: Leucine and lysine.

cards.front: What is the difference between a nucleoside and a nucleotide?
cards.back: A nucleoside has a base and sugar; a nucleotide also has one or more phosphate groups.

cards.front: Which bases are purines?
cards.back: Adenine and guanine, each with a fused two-ring structure.

cards.front: Which bases are pyrimidines?
cards.back: Cytosine, thymine, and uracil, each with a single ring.

cards.front: What sugar difference distinguishes RNA from DNA?
cards.back: RNA has ribose with a 2-prime hydroxyl; DNA has deoxyribose with hydrogen at that position.

cards.front: What bonds link nucleotides along a nucleic acid strand?
cards.back: 3-prime to 5-prime phosphodiester bonds.

cards.front: What does antiparallel mean for a DNA double helix?
cards.back: One strand runs 5-prime to 3-prime while its partner runs 3-prime to 5-prime.

cards.front: Which base pairs are canonical in double-stranded DNA?
cards.back: Adenine with thymine and guanine with cytosine.

cards.front: How many hydrogen bonds are in canonical A-T and G-C pairs?
cards.back: Two in A-T and three in G-C.

cards.front: Why is RNA more susceptible than DNA to alkaline hydrolysis?
cards.back: Its 2-prime hydroxyl can attack the neighboring phosphate backbone.

cards.front: In which direction do DNA and RNA polymerases synthesize nucleic acids?
cards.back: 5-prime to 3-prime by extending the growing strand's 3-prime hydroxyl.

cards.front: What does semiconservative DNA replication mean?
cards.back: Each daughter double helix contains one parental strand and one newly synthesized strand.

cards.front: Why does DNA polymerase need a primer?
cards.back: It needs an existing base-paired 3-prime hydroxyl to extend.

cards.front: What are Okazaki fragments?
cards.back: Short DNA segments synthesized on the lagging strand and later joined.

cards.front: What does DNA ligase repair during replication?
cards.back: Nicks in the sugar-phosphate backbone between adjacent DNA fragments.

cards.front: What does helicase do during DNA replication?
cards.back: Unwinds the double helix by separating paired strands.

cards.front: What does topoisomerase relieve during DNA replication?
cards.back: Torsional strain and supercoiling through transient DNA backbone cleavage and resealing.

cards.front: What is a codon?
cards.back: A three-nucleotide sequence in mRNA specifying an amino acid or a translation stop signal.

cards.front: What is the usual translation start codon?
cards.back: AUG, coding for methionine; bacterial initiation uses a formylated methionine.

cards.front: What are the three standard stop codons?
cards.back: UAA, UAG, and UGA.

cards.front: What does degeneracy of the genetic code mean?
cards.back: Multiple codons can specify the same amino acid.

cards.front: What does aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase do?
cards.back: Uses ATP to attach the appropriate amino acid to its corresponding tRNA.

cards.front: Which ribosomal site holds the growing peptide's tRNA before peptide transfer?
cards.back: The P site; the incoming aminoacyl-tRNA normally enters the A site.

cards.front: What catalyzes peptide bond formation in the ribosome?
cards.back: Ribosomal RNA in the large subunit's peptidyl transferase center.

cards.front: What are three major processing steps for a typical eukaryotic pre-mRNA?
cards.back: Addition of a 5-prime cap, splicing, and cleavage followed by polyadenylation at the 3-prime end.

cards.front: What does alternative splicing allow?
cards.back: Different mature mRNAs and protein isoforms to be produced from one gene.

cards.front: What does reverse transcriptase synthesize?
cards.back: DNA using an RNA template.

cards.front: What does PCR amplify?
cards.back: A selected DNA region using repeated denaturation, primer annealing, and polymerase extension.

cards.front: What does SDS-PAGE primarily separate proteins by?
cards.back: Polypeptide size after denaturation and roughly uniform charge-to-mass coating by SDS.

cards.front: What does a reducing agent add to an SDS-PAGE preparation?
cards.back: It breaks disulfide bonds, allowing disulfide-linked subunits to separate.

cards.front: What does isoelectric focusing separate proteins by?
cards.back: Isoelectric point, as proteins migrate through a pH gradient until their net charge is zero.

cards.front: What does size-exclusion chromatography separate molecules by?
cards.back: Hydrodynamic size; larger molecules generally elute first because they enter fewer pores.

cards.front: What does affinity chromatography exploit?
cards.back: Specific binding between the target molecule and an immobilized ligand.

cards.front: What does a Western blot detect?
cards.back: A specific protein using antibody binding after separation and transfer to a membrane.

cards.front: What does a Southern blot detect?
cards.back: Specific DNA sequences by hybridization with a complementary probe.

cards.front: What does a Northern blot detect?
cards.back: Specific RNA sequences by hybridization with a complementary probe.
